t: Quechua, a family of closely related languages that grew in central Peru in the first millennium CE, became the common language of the Inca empire, which carried it along the Andes from Ecuador to Chile.
After the Spanish conquest, missionaries used it to preach across the Andes, spreading it further than ever, and it was written in the Latin alphabet in grammars, sermons, chronicles and plays.
Spoken today by millions of people in six countries, it is the most widely spoken Indigenous language family of the Americas, and words such as llama, condor, puma and quinoa come from it.
dyk: English words such as llama, condor, puma, coca, quinoa and guano come from Quechua, and so does jerky, from ch’arki, the dried meat that sustained Andean travellers.
ev: The Wari state of the central Andes may have carried early Quechua across much of Peru
The Inca ruler Pachacuti begins the expansion that makes Quechua the language of an empire, by tradition
Domingo de Santo Tomás publishes the first grammar and dictionary of Quechua
A catechism in Spanish, Quechua and Aymara becomes the first book printed in South America
The Huarochirí Manuscript records the myths and rituals of an Andean province in Quechua
Felipe Guaman Poma de Ayala completes his illustrated chronicle of Andean life, with passages in Quechua
Peru makes Quechua an official language
A doctoral thesis written entirely in Quechua is defended for the first time, at the University of San Marcos in Lima

f.family: Quechuan: a family of closely related Andean languages, long in contact with the Aymaran languages
f.script: No writing before the Spanish conquest, when the Incas kept records on knotted cords, the khipu; the Latin alphabet since the 16th century
f.earliest: The grammar and dictionary of the Dominican friar Domingo de Santo Tomás, published in 1560
f.status: Spoken by perhaps 8 million people in Peru, Bolivia, Ecuador, Argentina, Colombia and Chile; official in Peru and Bolivia
